Information for students who have come to study in Korea.

First, international students must register as foreigners within 90 days of entering Korea. It is a good idea to carry your alien registration card at all times.

Second, you apply for the dormitory before the semester starts. When looking for a room off campus, it is best to use a real estate agency. Be sure to ask whether there is internet, a washing machine and a fridge.

Third, a transport card is convenient for buses and the underground. You also get a discount when you transfer.

Fourth, recyclable waste, food waste and general waste must be thrown away separately.

Finally, don't worry alone — ask seniors or friends. If you join a club, you can easily make Korean friends.

Everyone has at least one habit they would like to break. Some people bite their nails when they are nervous; others always put things off until tomorrow.

Breaking a bad habit is not easy. Many people practise what they decided for only a few days and then give up. That is why many people now say that small habits matter more than big plans.

For example, instead of ‘exercise for an hour every day’, you start with ‘drink a glass of water as soon as I get up’. It is so easy that it is hard to fail. Doing such a small thing every day gives you confidence, and little by little you can build bigger habits.

Writing your plan on paper and putting it somewhere visible, or telling a friend, is also a good method. Ask a friend to nag you when you are about to give up. In the end, the people who change their habits are not those who do well from the start but those who do not give up.

Long ago there lived a very lazy child. This child had a habit of lying down as soon as he finished eating. His mother always said, “If you lie down right after eating, you'll turn into a cow,” and asked him to help with the work, but he did not listen.

One day the child woke up and found he really had become a cow. As a cow he had to work in the field all day and could not rest. It was so hard that he cried and made up his mind to break his habit.

Then the child woke up. It had all been a dream. After that he broke his lazy habit and became more hard-working than anyone.

Active: someone does something **to** a thing — 문**을** 닫아요. Passive: the thing is the subject and takes **이/가** — 문**이** 닫**혀**요. Korean makes many passives by putting **-이-, -히-, -리-, -기-** inside the verb. Which one a verb takes has to be learned.
These two are everywhere. **보이다** = can be seen: 창문으로 바다가 **보여요**. **들리다** = can be heard: 잘 안 **들려요**. 좀 크게 말씀해 주세요. Korean does not say “I can see” with 볼 수 있다 here — the thing itself “is seen”.

One action is **completed**, and then something opposite or unexpected follows — often it is undone: **껐다가** 다시 켜 보세요 (turn it off and then on again). 코트를 **입었다가** 더워서 벗었어요. 가게에 **갔다가** 문이 닫혀 있어서 다시 왔어요.

**Same subject** in both halves. The verbs often come in opposite pairs: 켜다 ↔ 끄다, 입다 ↔ 벗다, 가다 ↔ 오다, 열다 ↔ 닫다, 타다 ↔ 내리다, 쓰다 ↔ 지우다, 사다 ↔ 환불하다. Compare **-다가** (without 았/었): the first action is **interrupted** midway — 집에 가**다가** 친구를 만났어요.
The result is **not what you would expect** from the first half: 껐다가 다시 **켰는데도** 안돼요 (even though I turned it off and on, it doesn't work). It is -는데 + 도, so the forms are the same as for -는데.
**-지만** simply contrasts two facts. **-는데도** adds surprise or frustration: “in spite of that”. 아껴 쓰**는데도** 항상 생활비가 모자라요. It often goes with **분명히** (surely), **아무리 … -아도**, 계속, 또.
**손보다** = to fix up, give something a going-over: 두 번이나 **손봤는데도** 또 고장 났어요. **갈다** = to replace a worn part with a new one: 배터리를 **갈다**, 필터를 **갈다** (갈아요, 간 지).

A/V-더니 — I saw that…, and then / but now

You report something you **observed** earlier and what followed. Two uses. ① **Change / contrast**: 어제까지 잘되**더니** 오늘은 안돼요 (it worked until yesterday, but today it doesn't). ② **Cause → result**: 동생이 열심히 공부하**더니** 합격했어요. 며칠 동안 폭우가 내리**더니** 홍수가 났어요.

1. Attach **-더니** straight to the stem — no tense: 오**더니**, 춥**더니**, 조용하**더니**. 2. The subject is someone or something **you watched** — usually not “I”: ~~제가 공부하더니~~. 3. The second half is a fact — no command or suggestion. 4. Both halves are normally about the same subject or the same topic.

When **I** did something and then found a result, Korean uses a different form, **-았더니/었더니**: (제가) 약을 먹**었더니** 좋아졌어요. For now just recognise it — this unit practises -더니 about other people and things.

Until Hangeul was created, Koreans borrowed and used Chinese characters for a long time. But there were far too many characters and they were hard to learn. So most ordinary people, who had no time to study, could neither read nor write.

King Sejong the Great, the fourth king of Joseon, thought the people needed a script they could learn and use easily. However, scholars who valued Chinese characters opposed the making of a new script. Despite the scholars' strong opposition, King Sejong did not give up, and in 1443 he created the new letters.

The script was announced to the world in 1446 under the name ‘Hunminjeongeum’. It means ‘the correct sounds for teaching the people’. At first there were many who did not use the new letters. But because it was easy to learn, more and more people came to use it.

Today Hangeul is known as an excellent script that can write a great many sounds with just 24 letters — 14 consonants and 10 vowels. In Korea, 9 October has been made Hangeul Day to commemorate the creation of Hangeul.

History is full of passives: **만들어지다** (be created), **발표되다** (be announced), **세워지다** (be founded), **알려지다 / 알려져 있다** (be known), **정해지다** (be fixed). N + **되다** is the passive of N + 하다: 발표**하다** → 발표**되다**, 사용**하다** → 사용**되다**.
